title: The development of doctrine
hookLine: Newman: living ideas grow like a tree, staying themselves

lines: A CHILD, THEN A GROWN ADULT.
cards: An old photograph: a child on a doorstep, gap-toothed, in a too-big sweater. Then the same person decades later. The height, the face, the voice, all different.
And yet nobody at the family table doubts it's the same person. Something stayed while everything grew. Newman put a question like that to the whole Church.
The first Christians didn't use every word the Church uses now. So is today's Church a different thing wearing an old name? Or the same thing, grown up?

teach.h: WORDS THE FIRST CHRISTIANS NEVER USED.
teach.b: Newman wrote a long book about it, An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, in the months before he became Catholic. First, the problem. Some teachings were said in words the first Christians never used.
The creed says the Son is of one substance with the Father, a phrase that isn't in the Gospels. Did the Church add something new, or put into words what was there all along? Second, the image.
A living idea, Newman argued, grows the way living things grow: a seed becomes a tree. Jesus himself compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds come to rest.
The tree looks nothing like the seed, yet it is the same plant, and no other plant could come from that seed. Third, the sentence.

teach.h: HERE BELOW TO LIVE IS TO CHANGE.
teach.b: Newman wrote: "In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often." It does not say anything goes. Fourth, the test.
Ideas can also decay, the way a body can sicken instead of grow.
So Newman tried to describe how to tell a true development from a corruption: a true one keeps the same type and principles, and carries forward what came before instead of overturning it.
Catholic teaching today speaks of doctrine developing in this sense. Other Christians describe faithfulness over time in their own ways.

teach.h: TO BE PERFECT IS TO HAVE CHANGED OFTEN.
teach.b: For Newman, the question was not whether the Church had changed. It was whether it had stayed itself while growing.

how: Catholic theologians and teachers draw on Newman's idea of development when they explain how the Church's teaching is put into new words over the centuries while remaining faithful to what was handed down.

o: the Church has become something else.
a living idea grows, and can stay itself while growing.
games.why: Newman argued that living ideas grow like a seed into a tree, and offered ways to tell growth from decay.

practice: Think back to how you understood God, or goodness, or what matters, as a child, a picture, a prayer, a rule, and set it next to how you understand it today. What has changed, and what, under all that change, has stayed the same?
If you pray, give thanks for the growth; if you don't, notice the thread that runs from then to now.

wordCard.voice: Mustard seed. The image Jesus used for a growing kingdom, which Newman borrowed to explain how a true teaching can grow into something unrecognizable and still be the same plant.

carryVoice: Your line: to live is to change. The seed and the tree are one plant. Eight hundred ninety days now.
